body.text: To care for a silk saree, fold it flat instead of hanging it, wrap it in cotton or muslin, keep it away from damp and sunlight, and refold it along new lines every three or four months. When it needs cleaning, take it to a dry cleaner who handles traditional textiles. These habits prevent almost everything that ruins silk: yellowing, splits along the folds, mildew and tarnished zari.
Kept this way, a silk saree can outlast the person who first wore it and still look luminous decades later.
This guide is about silk. Cotton, chiffon, georgette and organza need different handling, which our guide to [caring for sarees of every fabric](/journal/how-to-care-for-sarees) covers.
How should you store silk sarees at home?

Fold them flat and keep them in a cupboard that is dry and dark. Hanging is fine for an evening but not for months. The weight of heavy silk pulls it out of shape, and a hanger leaves marks across the shoulder of the drape that do not come out. This matters most for Kanjeevaram and Banarasi sarees, whose weight and zari make them the most vulnerable.
Keep piles short. Sarees at the bottom of a tall stack are pressed for months, and their folds set hard.

Wrap each saree in soft cotton or muslin, or keep it in a cloth saree bag. Never use plastic covers. Plastic traps moisture, which causes yellowing and mildew, and over time it can react with the silk and the zari.
And never put a silk saree away straight after wearing it. Air it for a few hours first, so perspiration and perfume can leave the fabric.
How often should you refold a silk saree?
Every three or four months. Wherever silk is folded, the fibres are under strain, and over the years that strain becomes a permanent crease and eventually a split.

Take your sarees out, let them air in the shade for an hour or two, and fold them again so the lines fall in new places. It takes an afternoon a few times a year, and it does more for a saree's life than anything else here.
How do you stop zari from tarnishing?
Keep it dry and keep it away from chemicals. Real zari is silver, and it tarnishes when it meets moisture, perfume, deodorant or perspiration.

Let perfume and deodorant dry completely before you drape. When you store a saree with heavy zari, lay a sheet of acid free tissue or soft muslin over the zari so it does not rub against the silk beside it. A couple of silica gel sachets in the cupboard, not touching the fabric, keep the air dry.

images.alt: Zari border covered with acid free tissue before storage

body.text: How do you protect silk sarees in humid weather?

Humidity brings mildew and moths, and both do their damage quietly. Keep silica gel in the cupboard, air your sarees on dry days through the monsoon, and open the cupboard for an hour now and then to let the air move.

For moths, use natural deterrents such as dried neem leaves, cloves or cedar, placed near the sarees but not touching them. Avoid naphthalene balls. They can stain silk and leave a smell that takes months to fade.

images.alt: Dried neem leaves and a silica gel sachet beside folded silk sarees in a cupboard

body.text: Can you wash a silk saree at home?
Heavy silk and anything with zari should always be dry cleaned by someone who works with traditional textiles. That includes every Kanjeevaram and Banarasi.

Some light silks without zari can survive a gentle hand wash in cold water with a mild shampoo. Test a hidden corner for colour first. Never wring the saree. Press the water out, then dry it flat in the shade. If you are unsure, do not risk it.
How do you iron a silk saree?

Use the silk setting, iron on the reverse, and keep a thin cotton cloth between the iron and the saree. Do not spray water on silk, because it leaves marks. Lay zari borders face down on a soft towel and press lightly through the cloth, keeping the iron moving.
How do you remove a stain from a silk saree?
Act quickly and gently. Blot the stain with a dry cloth, working from the outside in, and do not rub. Do not use water, which leaves a ring on silk.

For a fresh oil stain, sprinkle talcum powder over it, leave it for a few hours, then brush it away softly. For anything else, take the saree to a dry cleaner soon and tell them what caused the stain. Avoid home remedies such as lemon, vinegar or salt. They can strip dye and damage zari.
What should you do when a preloved silk saree arrives?
Unwrap it and let it air for a few hours. Look at where it has been folded, then fold it along new lines. A saree that has sat the same way for years needs its creases moved.
Resist the urge to restore it. Softened silk and gently darkened zari are what a saree of that age should look like, and aggressive cleaning takes that away for good.
What can you do with old silk sarees you no longer wear?
A silk saree that has been kept well often has decades of wear left in it. If you have one sitting unworn in a cupboard, it may be exactly what someone else is looking for.

items.question: Should silk sarees be folded or hung?
items.answer: Folded. Hanging for long periods stretches heavy silk and leaves marks where the hanger sits.

items.question: How often should I refold my silk sarees?
items.answer: Every three or four months, along new lines each time.

items.question: Why do silk sarees turn yellow in storage?
items.answer: Usually because plastic covers trapped moisture, because perspiration or perfume was left in the fabric before it was put away, or because of light. Air a saree before storing it, wrap it in cotton, and keep the cupboard dark.

items.question: Can I use naphthalene balls with silk sarees?
items.answer: It is best not to. They can stain silk and leave a lasting smell. Dried neem leaves, cloves or cedar placed near the saree work well.

items.question: Can I wash a Kanjeevaram saree at home?
items.answer: It is safer not to. Kanjeevaram silk and its zari should be dry cleaned by a specialist.

items.question: How do I store a zari saree so it does not tarnish?
items.answer: Keep it dry, cover the zari with acid free tissue or muslin, and let perfume dry fully before you wear it.
